title: How to make wise decisions
subject: reading

paragraphs.text: Across cultures, wisdom has been considered one of the most revered human qualities. Although the truly wise may seem few and far between, empirical research examining wisdom suggests that it isn’t an exceptional trait possessed by a small handful of bearded philosophers after all – in fact, the latest studies suggest that most of us have the ability to make wise decisions, given the right context.

‘It appears that experiential, situational, and cultural factors are even more powerful in shaping wisdom than previously imagined,’ says Associate Professor Igor Grossmann of the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada. ‘Recent empirical findings from cognitive, developmental, social, and personality psychology cumulatively suggest that people’s ability to reason wisely varies dramatically across experiential and situational contexts. Understanding the role of suchcontextual factors offers unique insights into understanding wisdom in daily life, as well as how it can be enhanced and taught.’

It seems that it’s not so much that some people simply possess wisdom and others lack it, but that our ability to reason wisely depends on a variety of external factors. ‘It is impossible to characterize thought processes attributed to wisdom without considering the role of contextual factors,’ explains Grossmann. ‘In other words, wisdom is not solely an “inner quality” but rather unfolds as a function of situations people happen to be in. Some situations are more likely to promote wisdom than others.’

Coming up with a definition of wisdom is challenging, but Grossmann and his colleagues have identified four key characteristics as part of a framework of wise reasoning. One is intellectual humility or recognition of the limits of our own knowledge, and another is appreciation of perspectives wider than the issue at hand. Sensitivity to the possibility of change in social relations is also key, along with compromise or integration of different attitudes and beliefs.

Grossmann and his colleagues have also found that one of the most reliable ways to support wisdom in our own day-to-day decisions is to look at scenarios from a third-party perspective, as though giving advice to a friend. Research suggests that when adopting a first-person viewpoint we focus on ‘the focal features of the environment’ and when we adopt a third-person, ‘observer’ viewpoint we reason more broadly and focus more on interpersonal and moral ideals such as justice and impartiality. Looking at problems from this more expansive viewpoint appears to foster cognitive processes related to wise decisions.

What are we to do, then, when confronted with situations like a disagreement with a spouse or negotiating a contract at work, that require us to take a personal stake? Grossmann argues that even when we aren’t able to change the situation, we can still evaluate these experiences from different perspectives.

For example, in one experiment that took place during the peak of a recent economic recession, graduating college seniors were asked to reflect on their job prospects. The students were instructed to imagine their career either ‘as if you were a distant observer’ or ‘before your own eyes as if you were right there’. Participants in the group assigned to the ‘distant observer’ role displayed more wisdom-related reasoning (intellectual humility and recognition of change) than did participants in the control group.

In another study, couples in long-term romantic relationships were instructed to visualize an unresolved relationship conflict either through the eyes of an outsider or from their own perspective. Participants then discussed an incident with their partner for 10 minutes, after which they wrote down their thoughts about it. Couples in the ‘other’s eyes’ condition were significantly more likely to rely on wise reasoning – recognizing others’ perspectives and searching for a compromise – compared to the couples in the egocentric condition.
‘Ego-decentering promotes greater focus on others and enables a bigger picture, conceptual view of the experience, affording recognition of intellectual humility and change,’ says Grossmann.

We might associate wisdom with intelligence or particular personality traits, but research shows only a small positive relationship between wise thinking and crystallized intelligence and the personality traits of openness and agreeableness. ‘It is remarkable how much people can vary in their wisdom from one situation to the next, and how much stronger such contextual effects are for understanding the relationship between wise judgment and its social and affective outcomes as compared to the generalized “traits”,’ Grossmann explains. ‘That is, knowing how wisely a person behaves in a given situation is more informative for understanding their emotions or likelihood to forgive [or] retaliate as compared to knowing whether the person may be wise “in general”.’

groups.instruction:
Questions 27–30

Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.prompt: What point does the writer make in the first paragraph?

options.text: Wisdom appears to be unique to the human race.
A basic assumption about wisdom may be wrong.
Concepts of wisdom may depend on the society we belong to.
There is still much to be discovered about the nature of wisdom.

questions.explanation:
译文：作者在第一自然段里提出了哪个观点？

虽然问题句已经直接指明答案来自于第一段，但其实并无多大用处：因为本段一共只有两句话而已。其中对应答案的第二句较为长难，关于本句的详细分析，可以参见前文“佳句赏析”中的第一句。读懂句意对比所有选项后，可以确认答案应为B项：A basic assumption about wisdom may be wrong.（关于智慧的一个基本假设也许是错误的。）

另外三个选项的信息，实际都并未在第一段中提及。

A项：Wisdom appears to be unique to the human race.（智慧貌似是人类这个物种所独有的。）

C项：Concepts of wisdom may depend on the society we belong to.（对智慧的概念也许要有赖于我们所属的具体社会而定。）

D项：There is still much to be discovered about the nature of wisdom.（关于智慧的本质还存在许多有待发掘之处。）

questions.prompt: What does Igor Grossmann suggest about the ability to make wise decisions?

options.text: It can vary greatly from one person to another.
Earlier research into it was based on unreliable data.
The importance of certain influences on it was underestimated.
Various branches of psychology define it according to their own criteria.

questions.explanation:
译文：Igor Grossmann关于做出明智决定的能力提出了什么看法？

本题虽然没有像上一题那样直接指出去哪一段寻找，但在问题句中包含着大写人名这个明显定位信息；如果考生关注到了下一题出自第三段这个细节的话，则对于明确本题定位更有帮助。然而，要解题却并非只阅读包含人名的一句话即可，同样需要通读全段所有句意才能最终确认答案应为C项：The importance of certain influences on it was underestimated.（一些影响了这种能力的因素的重要性被低估了。）

A项：It can vary greatly from one person to another.（它在一个人身上与在另一个人身上可以有极大的不同。）本选项对应第二段第二句话，有着极强的迷惑性。如果单看这一句，特别是如果断章取义地只看后半句，确实说到了“每个人做出明智分析的能力可以有巨大不同”；然而选择题的难度恰恰在于往往要求考生通读定位全段、全面掌握段意表达后才能做出最佳选择。考生在整体了解第二段的内容后应当不难看出：Grossmann意在点出一些先前被人们忽视了的因素的实际重要性，而非强调每个人的能力不同。关于本项对应句的详细分析，可以参见前文“佳句赏析”中的第二句。

B项：Earlier research into it was based on unreliable data.（对它的早期研究是基于不可靠的数据。）本段只说到了近期的研究发现，完全未对之前的研究做任何评价。

D项：Various branches of psychology define it according to their own criteria.（各种心理学分支都按照自己的标准来定义它。）这个选项的信息完全不曾在原文中出现过。

questions.prompt: According to the third paragraph, Grossmann claims that the level of wisdom an individual shows

options.text: can be greater than they think it is.
will be different in different circumstances.
may be determined by particular aspects of their personality.
should develop over time as a result of their life experiences.

questions.explanation:
译文：根据第三段内容，Grossmann宣称一个人展现出来的智慧程度

本题的难度相对较低：有了上一段的内容铺垫后，考生从本段第一句话中就不难看出作者的意图走向。不过更为稳妥的做法当然是耐心看完另外两句话和对比全部选项，最终确定答案应为B项：will be different in different circumstances.（在不同的场合中将会是不一样的。）

本题中的另外三个选项，基本都属于“完全未在段中被提到”的类型，干扰性不大。

A项：can be greater than they think it is.（可以比他们自己所以为的更高。）

C项：may be determined by particular aspects of their personality.（也许是由他们性格中的某些特定方面所决定的。）

D项：should develop over time as a result of their life experiences.（应当作为他们生活经验的结果而随时间流逝不断发展。）

questions.prompt: What is described in the fifth paragraph?

options.text: a difficulty encountered when attempting to reason wisely
an example of the type of person who is likely to reason wisely
a controversial view about the benefits of reasoning wisely
a recommended strategy that can help people to reason wisely

questions.explanation:
译文：第五段描述了什么？

本题的解题难度主要来自于占据了大部分段落内容、结构比较复杂的第一和第二句话。关于这两句的详细分析，可以分别参见前文“佳句赏析”中的第三和第四句。阅读文意和对比过选项后，可知正确答案应为D项：a recommended strategy that can help people to reason wisely（一种能帮助人们进行明智分析的推荐策略）

考生只需看懂文意和另外三个选项本身的意思，就不难看出它们都并未在第五段中被提及过，基本不构成对答题的干扰。

A项：a difficulty encountered when attempting to reason wisely（当试图去进行明智分析时会遭遇到的困难）

B项：an example of the type of person who is likely to reason wisely（对于更有可能做出明智分析的一类人举个例子）

C项：a controversial view about the benefits of reasoning wisely（关于明智分析所具备好处的一个矛盾看法）

34. 本题的定位不难，一来是因为题干中的scenarios在文章中直接原词重现了，二来也是因为在解答前面的第30题时，考生理应已经阅读了本段内容，如果使用了平行阅读的方法则理应已经得出了本题和下一题的答案。原文给出的答案为third-party perspective，这个“第三方视角”在词库中的最佳对应项应为F objectivity。

35. 本题定位思路与上一道题类似，正确答案应为原文信息justice and impartiality在词库中的对应项G fairness。

groups.contextHtml:
The characteristics of wise reasoning

 

Igor Grossmann and colleagues have established four characteristics which enable us to make wise decisions. It is important to have a certain degree of [31] ______  regarding the extent of our knowledge, and to take into account [32] ______ which may not be the same as our own. We should also be able to take a broad [33] ______ of any situation. Another key characteristic is being aware of the likelihood of alterations in the way that people relate to each other.

 

Grossmann also believes that it is better to regard scenarios with [34] ______ . By avoiding the first-person perspective, we focus more on [35] ______ and on other moral ideals, which in turn leads to wiser decision-making.

groups.instruction:
Questions 36–40

Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 3?

In questions 36–40 on your answer sheet, choose

TRUE if the statement agrees with the information

FALSE if the statement contradicts the information

NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this

questions.prompt: Students participating in the job prospects experiment could choose one of two perspectives to take.
questions.explanation:
译文：参与工作前景实验的学生们可以自行选择两种角度中选择哪一种来思考。

本题的定位不难，考生可直接用原文重现的题干词job prospects找到第七段开头。但本题的解答却并不简单：首先是因为包含定位信息的句子本身并没有给出足够的解题信息，考生需耐心往下再读两句，才能看出第二句说的是参与试验的人分为两组，而到了第三句才对“他们的所属组是否出于个人选择”给出了相关信息；其次，还因为真正给出答题关键的第三句对于考生关注细节信息的要求极高，解题窍要全部体现在不起眼的assigned这一个词上。考生如果能根据题型特点耐心阅读，同时关注定位原文的细节表达，则可选出正确答案为FALSE。

questions.prompt: Participants in the couples experiment were aware that they were taking part in a study about wise reasoning.
questions.explanation:
译文：伴侣实验的参与者们明确知道他们是在参加一个关于做出明智分析的研究。

本题的定位其实不难，因为考生只需在解答上一道题后顺次向后文阅读，即可在下一段的开头找到couples这个原词重现的题干对应信息；然而读遍全段也并未看到与“参与者是否知道研究目的”相关的内容，可知答案应为NOT GIVEN。

questions.prompt: In the couples experiments, the length of the couples’ relationships had an impact on the results.
questions.explanation:
本题与上一题的定位出处一致，也不难寻找。虽然原文确实提到了这些实验参与者都有着“长时间的伴侣关系”，但却并未跟进提及这种时长是否影响了结果，因而对考生解答的干扰其实不大，可以判定本题的正确答案也是 NOT GIVEN。

本题和上一题给考生解题带来的难度，主要体现在连续出了两个“未提及”答案，需考生对于自己的阅读理解能力具备一定信心、确定所读文章着实不曾提及相关信息，从而避免考场上过于摇摆不定的心态、因为怀疑是自己的阅读定位出现问题而不必要地回读确认、浪费过多时间。

questions.prompt: In both experiments, the participants who looked at the situation from a more detached viewpoint tended to make wiser decisions.
questions.explanation:
译文：在两组实验中，从一个更客观疏离角度看待场景的参与者们往往都做出了更为明智的决定。

本题是一个比较少见的题目类型。在判断题这种“考查细节理解”是绝对主流要求的题型中，偶然也会出现一个较难定位到原文中具体某一句话、却结合了前文大意的很容易判断正误的题干信息。文中的两组实验都用充分的细节肯定了“采用客观视角”所带来的益处，因此考生只需认识题干中detached这个略陌生的词汇，即可得出正确答案应为TRUE。

questions.prompt: Grossmann believes that a person’s wisdom is determined by their intelligence to only a very limited extent.
questions.explanation:
译文：Grossmann相信，一个人的智慧与否只在一个非常有限的程度内取决于他们的智商。

本题的定位不难，一个重要原因在于经过前面的解答过程，只剩下有限的原文内容需要考生阅读寻找了。本题的直接对应为最后一段的第一句，不过如果能继续向后文再读一句，则可以更加肯定答案为TRUE。

articleHtml:
How to make wise decisions

 

Across cultures, wisdom has been considered one of the most revered human qualities. Although the truly wise may seem few and far between, empirical research examining wisdom suggests that it isn’t an exceptional trait possessed by a small handful of bearded philosophers after all – in fact, the latest studies suggest that most of us have the ability to make wise decisions, given the right context.

‘It appears that experiential, situational, and cultural factors are even more powerful in shaping wisdom than previously imagined,’ says Associate Professor Igor Grossmann of the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada. ‘Recent empirical findings from cognitive, developmental, social, and personality psychology cumulatively suggest that people’s ability to reason wisely varies dramatically across experiential and situational contexts. Understanding the role of suchcontextual factors offers unique insights into understanding wisdom in daily life, as well as how it can be enhanced and taught.’

It seems that it’s not so much that some people simply possess wisdom and others lack it, but that our ability to reason wisely depends on a variety of external factors. ‘It is impossible to characterize thought processes attributed to wisdom without considering the role of contextual factors,’ explains Grossmann. ‘In other words, wisdom is not solely an “inner quality” but rather unfolds as a function of situations people happen to be in. Some situations are more likely to promote wisdom than others.’

Coming up with a definition of wisdom is challenging, but Grossmann and his colleagues have identified four key characteristics as part of a framework of wise reasoning. One is intellectual humility or recognition of the limits of our own knowledge, and another is appreciation of perspectives wider than the issue at hand. Sensitivity to the possibility of change in social relations is also key, along with compromise or integration of different attitudes and beliefs.

Grossmann and his colleagues have also found that one of the most reliable ways to support wisdom in our own day-to-day decisions is to look at scenarios from a third-party perspective, as though giving advice to a friend. Research suggests that when adopting a first-person viewpoint we focus on ‘the focal features of the environment’ and when we adopt a third-person, ‘observer’ viewpoint we reason more broadly and focus more on interpersonal and moral ideals such as justice and impartiality. Looking at problems from this more expansive viewpoint appears to foster cognitive processes related to wise decisions.

What are we to do, then, when confronted with situations like a disagreement with a spouse or negotiating a contract at work, that require us to take a personal stake? Grossmann argues that even when we aren’t able to change the situation, we can still evaluate these experiences from different perspectives.

For example, in one experiment that took place during the peak of a recent economic recession, graduating college seniors were asked to reflect on their job prospects. The students were instructed to imagine their career either ‘as if you were a distant observer’ or ‘before your own eyes as if you were right there’. Participants in the group assigned to the ‘distant observer’ role displayed more wisdom-related reasoning (intellectual humility and recognition of change) than did participants in the control group.

In another study, couples in long-term romantic relationships were instructed to visualize an unresolved relationship conflict either through the eyes of an outsider or from their own perspective. Participants then discussed an incident with their partner for 10 minutes, after which they wrote down their thoughts about it. Couples in the ‘other’s eyes’ condition were significantly more likely to rely on wise reasoning – recognizing others’ perspectives and searching for a compromise – compared to the couples in the egocentric condition.

‘Ego-decentering promotes greater focus on others and enables a bigger picture, conceptual view of the experience, affording recognition of intellectual humility and change,’ says Grossmann.

We might associate wisdom with intelligence or particular personality traits, but research shows only a small positive relationship between wise thinking and crystallized intelligence and the personality traits of openness and agreeableness. ‘It is remarkable how much people can vary in their wisdom from one situation to the next, and how much stronger such contextual effects are for understanding the relationship between wise judgment and its social and affective outcomes as compared to the generalized “traits”,’ Grossmann explains. ‘That is, knowing how wisely a person behaves in a given situation is more informative for understanding their emotions or likelihood to forgive [or] retaliate as compared to knowing whether the person may be wise “in general”.’
